title: Burst resonance mapping — transient tail experiments
content:
OVERVIEW:
Quick personal notes from the small series of experiments probing transient tail events that look a lot like a resonance: repeated short bursts at particular spacing that amplify p99/p999 latency. Goal was to map the pattern space (burst size, inter-burst spacing, baseline qps) and see how KV-cache + batching window interact with oscillatory queues.

HIGH-LEVEL HYPOTHESIS:
- When evenly spaced micro-bursts align with the batching/window timing and KV cache miss hotspots, we see constructive interference: spikes get longer and amplify across the downstream queue (resonance).
- Small changes to batch window (5ms -> 2ms) or pre-warm thresholds reduce amplitude significantly.

ENVIRONMENT / SETUP:
- Model: llama2-13b-4bit-quant (runtime variant: v2025-10-optim1)
- Hardware: 1x A100-80GB per replica (dedicated dev pool, no multi-tenancy)
- Serving runtime: local branch runtime/feature/resonance-probe (PR 812)
- Clients: synthetic driver on k8s job (k8s-jobs/probe-runner)
- Baseline cold/warm: cache primed with 200 unique prefixes before each run unless noted
- Batch settings: dynamic batching on, target batch size 32, max latency window 5ms default (we sweep to 2ms/10ms/20ms)
- Concurrency: single-stream (1 request per connection) but we drive multiple parallel clients to control arrival patterns
- Measurement: p50/p90/p95/p99/p999 (wall ms), end-to-end including routing + queueing + token generation for first 128 tokens

TRAFFIC PATTERNS TESTED (named for shorthand):
- Poisson baseline: mean qps 80 (control)
- Microburst-64x@10s: 64 requests fired at t=0 every 10s (repeat 50 cycles)
- Wave-32@300ms-gap: 32 req every 300ms for 30s (dense short wave)
- Resonant-sweep: sweep inter-burst gap 50ms-1000ms with burst size fixed at 48
- Staggered-cascade: 3 upstream sources offset by 100ms each, each sending 24 req bursts every 5s

KEY OBSERVATIONS (raw-ish):
- Poisson baseline (qps 80): p99 ~ 42ms, p999 ~ 98ms (warm cache). Stable, no tails.
- Microburst-64x@10s: immediate p99 jump during burst to 390-540ms depending on batch window, p999 up to ~1.9s for 2/3 of runs. Recovery time > 2s in some cycles (queueing oscillation).
- Wave-32@300ms-gap: sustained elevated p95/p99 during the entire wave (p99 ~ 650ms), but no long tails after wave stops (fast drain).
- Resonant-sweep: strong peak in tail amplitude when inter-burst gap ~ equal to batch-window multiples (observed peaks at ~5ms, ~315ms, ~630ms). Suggests alignment with both batching and internal KV-cache eviction/repopulation rhythm.
- Staggered-cascade: worst-case — offsets caused overlapping windows and produced very long tails (p999 > 3s); seen repeated across runs.

DETAILED RUN NOTES (examples):
- Run R-12 (burst 64, gap 10s, batch-window 5ms): p50 38ms, p95 120ms, p99 420ms, p999 1.2s. KV-hit-rate dropped from 0.96->0.72 during burst (cache set thrash). Observed many small kernel launch spikes (GPU occupancy oscillation).
- Run R-15 (same but window=2ms): p99 reduced to 210ms, p999 to 540ms. Lower batching window reduced constructive build-up. However tail still present — likely cache eviction still a factor.
- Run R-23 (window=20ms): p99 ballooned to 880ms and p999 to 2.1s — larger window allowed bigger batches and bigger scheduling pauses, so burst created big latent queue.

INSTRUMENTATION NOTES (what we measured/what's missing):
- Measured: request arrival timestamps, queue entry/exit, batch sizes, per-token latency, KV-cache hit/miss per request, cuda kernel times (coarse), GPU utilization per 100ms.
- Missing (to add): per-request memory allocation events; fine-grained kernel queue depths; eviction timings from KV cache (we currently only log hit/miss but not eviction timestamps). Also need to correlate upstream load balancer batching at the proxy layer (observed some client-side coalescing).

QUICK DIAGNOSTIC TAKEAWAYS:
- Two dominant mechanisms for resonance: (1) batching window alignment (bigger windows => more opportunity for bursts to form large batches and then cause long serialization), (2) KV-cache thrash causing extra per-request work (cache repopulation costs amplified when many distinct prefixes arrive together).
- Small windows (2-3ms) help but do not eliminate long-tail if cache hit-rate collapses.
- Pre-warming the set of likely prefixes before burst dramatically reduces p999 (e.g., pre-warm 500 prefixes => p999 reduced 80% on identical bursts). Practical? depends on customer workload predictability.

QUANTITATIVE RULE-OF-THUMB (from runs):
- If burst_size * avg_token_time > batch_window * X where X~10-20, expect brewing tail. (Need to formalize formula)
- KV-hit-rate threshold: when hit-rate < 0.85 during burst we observe >3x inflation in p99 vs baseline.

ACTIONABLES / NEXT STEPS:
1) Add eviction logging for KV cache (timestamped evict/insert) so we can directly see thrash windows. (blocked: infra trace change, assigned Ari)
2) Run controlled tests with synthetic deterministic prefixes vs fully random to isolate cache effect (sprint: 1 day).
3) Try adaptive small-window policy: shrink batch-window when microburst detected (prototype in PR 812 but needs stable tests).
4) Evaluate proactive prefetch strategy for top-N prefixes during expected burst windows (simulate predictions).
5) Add synthetic upstream jitter to simulate client-side coalescing; check sensitivity.

OPEN QUESTIONS / THINGS TO WATCH:
- Is this resonance visible in multi-tenant shared pools or did dedicated dev pool simplify behaviour? I think multi-tenant amplifies due to noisy neighbors and differing patterns. Need to test on a mixed-tenancy staging pool.
- Long-term tradeoff: small windows reduce tails but increase per-token overhead (more small kernels). Need actual cost model.
- Could placement (packing requests on GPU) be altered to favor smaller, parallel micro-batches instead of one large serialized batch? Might reduce max tail but change throughput.

NOTES TO SELF (rough):
- When writing up, include a simple timeline chart: x-axis time(ms), show arrival bursts, queue length, batch sizes over time, and KV hit-rate overlay. That visual makes it obvious.
- Keep one run with GPU profile enabled (nvidia tools) to inspect kernel queuing — probably reveals scheduling stalls.

CONCLUSION (scratch):
- Resonant tails are not a single-point bug; emergent property of batching + cache + arrival spacing. Mitigations exist at multiple layers: batching policy, cache pre-warm/prefetch, placement. Short-term wins: shrink batch window adaptively + targeted pre-warm. Medium-term: smarter cache eviction/placement + predictive prefetch.
